title: Kitchen and sword
hookLine: may the kitchen that feeds and the sword that protects both prevail
last: NAAM DAAN — THE NAME ABOVE ALL.

lines: A POT WIDE ENOUGH FOR A CHILD.
cards: A huge iron pot, wide enough for a child to sit in, sits on a fire behind a gurdwara, with dal bubbling in it for five hundred people.
Then there's a sword, a real one, curved, hanging on the wall of a Sikh home or carried in procession at Vaisakhi. They look like opposites: one for feeding, the other for fighting.
And yet the Ardas puts them side by side, in three short words, and asks for both of them to win. Day six hundred twenty-two remembered the people who ran the pot and wielded the sword.
Now the Ardas makes those two things a single prayer.

teach.b: Just before the gifts, the Ardas says: jahaan jahaan khaalsaa jee saahib, tahaan tahaan rachhiaa riaait. In paraphrase: wherever the Khalsa is, there may there be protection and grace. Then three words: deg tegh fateh.
Deg is the big cooking cauldron, the pot of the langar.

teach.h: DEG: THE POT. TEGH: THE SWORD.
teach.b: Tegh is the sword. Fateh, from the opening greeting, is victory. May the kitchen and the sword be victorious.
The deg stands for feeding: the free kitchen, open to anyone, where everyone sits on the same floor. The tegh stands for protecting: standing up for those who can't stand up for themselves.

teach.h: TWO WAYS OF CARING FOR PEOPLE.
teach.b: Sikhs would say they aren't opposites at all, but two ways of caring for people. One keeps them alive; the other keeps them safe. A community that only feeds can't protect the people it feeds.
A community that only fights forgets why it fights. So the Ardas asks for both to prevail, together. The phrase is old.
Deg, tegh and fateh appear together on Sikh seals and coins from the 1700s on, and the words have been a kind of motto ever since.
And the order: deg comes first.
The kitchen before the sword, just as in the line about the steadfast: those who shared, ran the pot, and wielded the sword.
The Ardas then goes on, in paraphrase: may the honor of the tradition be kept, may the Panth be victorious, may the sword help us, may the Khalsa's word stand high. And then come the gifts.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs ask that wherever the Khalsa is there be protection and grace, and that deg and tegh, the langar's cauldron and the sword, prevail together.

o: victory, asked for the pot and the sword
the sword carried in a Vaisakhi procession
a greeting said only at the end of a war

games.q: kitchen and sword — tap the pairs.

s: Sikhs see the pot and the sword as opposites
they're two ways of caring for people: feeding and protecting.
in deg teg fateh, the kitchen comes before the sword
deg first, as in the line about those who ran the pot and wielded the sword.

games.q: your community can only fund one thing this year: a free kitchen, or volunteers who protect people in danger. what does deg teg fateh say?
o: ask for both to prevail, the kitchen first.
games.why: the Ardas refuses to choose: may the kitchen and the sword both win. one keeps people alive, the other keeps them safe.

practice: Think of someone who could use a meal, a snack or a cup of tea, a coworker skipping lunch, a neighbor, a tired parent, and picture handing it to them.
Then think of someone who could use protecting, a person being talked over, a kid being picked on, and picture standing next to them. Feeding and protecting, side by side; if you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Fateh, victory: the pot and the sword, both asked to be victorious together, feeding and protecting, the kitchen first.
